reasoning: The paper is a clinical neuroimaging study generating new PET and MRI data (11C-PBR28, 18F-flortaucipir, cortical thickness) and neuropathology data from patients with svPPA and healthy controls, which constitutes newly generated research data (D1). For software, the authors used existing established tools (Freesurfer, PMOD, SPM12, MATLAB curve fitting toolbox, IBM SPSS) for processing and analysis, but did not create or significantly extend any new software - these are existing research/generic software packages used as utilities, fitting S2 (or S3 for purely generic tools like SPSS/MATLAB fitting). Since some of these (Freesurfer, PMOD, SPM12) are specialized research software tools used without modification, this is best classified as S2 (software used) rather than S3.

The paper uses existing research software (SNANA for simulations, PSNID classifier, SALT2 light-curve fitter, emcee MCMC sampler, CosmoMC) but does not claim to create new general-purpose software packages—though they do release their BEAMS implementation code on GitHub/Zenodo, this is more of an analysis script extending existing SNANA infrastructure rather than a significant new software contribution claimed as a primary output; the core software (SNANA, SALT2, emcee, CosmoMC) is existing/used software, with modest additions (new CC SN templates added to SNANA library) that don't rise to the level of claiming software generation as a primary contribution. For data, the paper clearly generates substantial new research data: they conducted an extensive host galaxy redshift follow-up survey (3147 new spectroscopic redshifts), generated large Monte Carlo SN simulations (25 simulations x 1000+ SNe), and created new CC SN templates for SNANA. This is clear data generation (D1). The software used (SNANA, SALT2, emcee, CosmoMC, PSNID) is existing, established research software used as tools rather than being the generated contribution of this paper, hence S2.

The paper uses standard/generic statistical software (R with mgcv package) for analysis, which is a utility tool not claimed as a research contribution - this falls under S3 (no research software generated or used as a contribution). The study generates new research data through an experimental infestation study: blood samples, genotyping, immunological assays (ELISA, flow cytometry, proliferation assays) collected from 30+ cattle over 13 weeks, which constitutes newly generated research data (D1).

This is a purely conceptual/theoretical paper that analyzes literature on bureaucracy and the Balanced Scorecard to propose a conceptual framework. It does not involve the creation or use of any research software, nor does it collect, generate, or use any research data (no empirical case studies, surveys, or datasets). The paper explicitly states it offers no empirical support and calls for future case-study research. Hence it falls under No Software, No Data.

This is a review/survey paper that synthesizes and discusses existing literature on energy storage for water desalination systems powered by renewable energy. It does not develop or significantly extend any research software, nor does it use existing software as part of a reported methodology. It also does not generate new research data (no experiments, simulations, or measurements performed by the authors) nor does it use a specific existing dataset to derive new findings—rather it reviews and summarizes findings, numbers, and conclusions reported in other studies. The paper is purely a narrative literature review with no software or data artifacts created or used by the authors themselves.

The paper uses existing software tools (Weka, JADBio) for machine learning analysis without claiming to create or extend new software - these are applied as analysis tools (S2). The research generates new data in two ways: (1) the AAA assessment dataset of 192 patients used for ML analysis, and more importantly (2) a novel autism screening questionnaire (ASTA) was developed and administered to 30 and 18 patients respectively, generating new survey/assessment data specifically for this research. This constitutes clear data generation (D1), as the paper describes creating new screening tools and collecting original patient response data through them, going beyond simply using existing datasets.

The paper uses existing/standard tools (MATLAB, LABVIEW) as implementation platforms for the algorithm rather than claiming to develop new research software as a contribution - these are generic computational tools used to run the proposed MILP optimization, ANFIS forecasting and RTPC control algorithm, so this is S2 (software used). However, the paper clearly generates research data: it creates forecasted load/PV profiles with injected noise (MAPE 3.6%), experimental measurement data from the laboratory microgrid (SOC curves, power drawn profiles, forecasting accuracy tables), and results from simulations across four seasons. This generated/derived data (experimental and simulation outputs) qualifies as D1 (data generated), since the paper creates new recorded data through experiments and simulation beyond just using pre-existing datasets (the CREST model data and weather data were used as inputs, but new simulation/experimental output data was generated).

The study generated new research data: raw field recordings and 360° videos were collected in Peace Gardens, Sheffield, and edited into four experimental soundscape samples, plus survey/questionnaire data (SQE, LoW scores) from 120 participants, which are openly deposited on Mendeley Data. This constitutes generated research data (D1). Software used includes Adobe Audition (editing), SPSS and Matlab (statistical/clustering analysis) - these are generic, widely-used commercial tools used as utilities for data processing/analysis rather than research software created or significantly extended by the authors, so this falls under S3 (no research software contribution).

The study generated original behavioral observation data on two Palawan binturong via CCTV monitoring (an activity budget dataset collected specifically for this research), which qualifies as research data generated (D1). Statistical analysis was performed using R, a generic statistical programming environment used as a utility (not developed or extended as part of the research), so this falls under S3 (no research software claimed). Excel was also used only as a data entry tool, not as research software.

This is a post-hoc analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial (SSaSS) that generated new research data - cancer outcome data (stomach cancer, other cancer events) from trial participants collected through follow-up, hospitalization records, and death adjudication. This represents newly generated research data (clinical trial outcome data) rather than reuse of existing external datasets. The statistical analysis was performed using SAS software, which is a generic/commercial statistical software package not developed or extended by the researchers, falling under the 'Not Research Software' category (similar to STATA). No custom software, scripts, or tools were created or claimed as a contribution. Therefore this is S3 (No Research Software) and D1 (Research Data Generated).

The paper uses established research software tools (SPM12/DCM10, FreeSurfer, FSL, 3D Slicer, SEEGA) for analysis but does not claim to have developed or significantly extended any of these software packages, so it falls under S2 (Software Used). The study generates original research data: EEG-fMRI recordings, BOLD maps, DCM connectivity models, and clinical/outcome data collected from 10 patients specifically for this study, which clearly constitutes newly generated research data (D1).

This is a review/perspective article synthesizing findings from existing GWAS and Mendelian randomisation studies on type 2 diabetes and cancer. It does not report generating or using any specific software tool, nor does it generate or analyse its own primary research data - it discusses and summarizes results (findings/associations) from previously published studies without claiming creation of new datasets or software. Hence it falls under No Software, No Data.

The paper develops a conceptual process-optimization model (smart lean-green) validated through two real-world case studies (automobile and mining machinery shop floors). Data was collected via Gemba walks, brainstorming sessions, interviews, and production measurements (lead time, uptime, production rate, etc.), which constitutes newly generated research data from fieldwork observations. No research software was created or used as a contribution; mentions of 'design software' are only suggested future actions, not implemented/used software. Thus this is No Software, Data Generated (S3D1).

The paper uses the existing Russian Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS) panel data (2002-2019), an existing dataset not created by the authors, which qualifies as D2 (data used). The study employs standard econometric methods (fixed-effects regressions, ordered logit with BUC estimator by Baetschmann et al. 2020) implemented presumably via Stata commands (e.g., feologit), which is existing research software used for estimation rather than software created/extended by the authors - qualifying as S2 (software used). There is no claim of generating new software or new datasets.

This is a pure mathematics paper on matrix theory, presenting theorems and proofs about symmetry decompositions of matrices and their pseudoinverses. It uses the Wilson matrix purely as a numerical example to illustrate theoretical results, but this is not research data in the sense of collected/generated data supporting empirical findings - it's a standard mathematical test matrix used for illustrative computation. No software is created, extended, or used as a research contribution (any numerical computation like SVD is incidental/utility). The paper explicitly states "No data was used for the research described in the article." There is no claim of software creation or use as research software, and no research data generated or used.

The paper uses an existing numerical model/code (described in Willis et al. 2007, "available on request") to run a suite of rotating convection simulations - the code itself is not claimed as a new or significantly extended contribution, but rather an existing tool applied to new parameter regimes, so it is S2 (software used). The paper generates extensive simulation output data (model/simulation inputs and outputs) which constitutes newly created research data (D1) - 68+ simulations with heat flux heterogeneity patterns, temperature fields, velocity fields, etc. The data availability statement explicitly says data is available from the corresponding author, confirming it was generated by this research.

The paper uses existing publicly available long-read sequencing data (NABEC cohort, accessed via AnVIL) as well as reference genome/database resources (DGV, UniProt, BLAST), and performs analyses deriving structural variant characterizations and phylogenies - this counts as using existing research data (D2), not generating new raw data. The paper uses established bioinformatics tools (Sniffles2, RepeatMasker, EMBOSS, MAFFT, IQ-TREE2, Ensembl, BLAST, RIdeogram, Plotrix, Napu pipeline) but does not claim to have created or significantly extended any software - all tools are used as existing research software for analysis purposes (S2). No novel software/pipeline was developed by the authors.

The paper uses existing surveillance and traveler data (laboratory-confirmed MERS cases, travel volume statistics, population sizes) to derive estimates via a mathematical formula, but does not generate new primary data (it uses existing WHO/CDC/travel datasets) nor does it create or extend any research software—calculations are based on a formula from a prior study, not a novel computational tool. Thus it's data used (D2) with no software developed or used as a contribution (S3).

This is an empirical parasitology/histopathology study where researchers collected shark specimens, dissected copepods, and generated new histological data (slides, images, observations of pathology) - this constitutes newly generated research data (specimens deposited in museum collection, histological sections). No research software is created or used/claimed as a contribution - only standard lab equipment (autostainer) and no computational analysis tools are mentioned. Thus it falls under No Software, Data Generated.

The paper generates substantial new research data: 44 lytic flavophage isolates, their genome sequences, metagenomes, TEM images, and bacterial host genomes - all newly produced through the research (D1). Regarding software, the authors used a variety of existing bioinformatics tools (SPAdes, Tadpole, Bandage, PhageTerm, VirClust, ViPTree, VICTOR, MUSCLE, IQ-Tree, BLASTN, WIsH, CRISPRCasFinder, ARB, RAxML, MiGA) but did not claim to develop new software or significantly extend any of these tools within this paper (S2). Thus the paper fits S2D1.

The paper conducts an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study, generating synthetic data under various model misspecification scenarios (local dependence, nonnormal latent distributions) - this constitutes generated research data (D1). For software, the authors use existing general-purpose statistical tools (R's 'optim' function, 'NumDeriv' package, 'ltm' package) to implement their custom computations, but there is no claim of having created or significantly extended a research software package/tool as a research contribution in itself - they used existing R functions/packages to perform estimation and numerical derivatives (S2). They also apply their methods to a real dataset (used data), reinforcing D1 since generated data is prioritized when both generated and used. Thus the classification is S2D1.

The paper describes the creation of a novel online software tool (the Cool Farm Biodiversity metric), which constitutes research software generated for the purpose of this research - a significant new tool built through expert elicitation and evidence synthesis, not merely use of existing software. Alongside software development, the authors generated substantial new research data: expert judgement scores, evidence assessment scores (via a modified Delphi process), and a newly structured scoring database (provided as Supplementary Table S12) covering actions, species groups, and biomes. They also present example farm data (hypothetical and real) illustrating outputs. This generated dataset of scores and metric parameters is original research data produced through the study's expert elicitation process, going beyond simple software outputs to include newly created structured data. Hence both software and data were generated by the research.

The paper reports experimental synthesis and characterization of solid dispersions (PXRD, DSC, FTIR, dissolution) generating new research data from these experiments - clearly D1 as new data was created. Software used (EVA, TA universal analysis, OMNIC) are standard commercial instrument analysis tools used as utilities for data processing/analysis, not claimed as research contributions or developed/extended by the authors, so this falls under S3 (no research software).

This is a historical/architectural humanities paper using archival documents, letters, exhibition catalogues, and secondary literature as evidence for a narrative argument. It does not involve any research software (no code, tools, or computational methods created or used), nor does it generate or use research data in the sense defined (e.g., structured datasets, measurements, surveys). The archival letters and catalogues are treated as historical sources/literature rather than research data to be analyzed statistically. Thus it falls into No Software, No Data (S3D3).

This is a scoping review that systematically searched databases and synthesized findings from 7 included clinical studies on fluoride mouthwashes' effects on orthodontic appliances. No research software was created or used beyond generic tools (Excel for data charting, EndNote for duplicate removal), which are utility/generic tools not counted as research software (S3). The paper uses existing research data in the form of findings/results extracted from the included primary studies (data charting, risk of bias assessment, synthesis of results), which constitutes using existing research data rather than generating new data (D2).

This is a crystal structure determination paper (IUCrData). The researchers synthesized a new compound and generated crystallographic data (atomic coordinates, bond lengths, hydrogen-bond geometry, CIF data) via X-ray diffraction - this is newly generated research data (D1). For software, they used established crystallographic tools (APEX3, SAINT, SADABS, SHELXT, SHELXL, DIAMOND) which are existing research software packages used for data collection and structure refinement, not created or extended by the authors (S2).

The paper used NVivo, a generic qualitative data analysis software package (used as a utility for coding, not created or extended as a research contribution), placing it at S2/S3 boundary - but since it's merely a utility tool for processing data (similar to generic data processing software), this is S3 level usage. However, the paper generated original research data: interview transcripts and focus group recordings from 22 teachers were newly collected and analyzed as part of this evaluation study, which constitutes generated research data (D1). Since NVivo is a widely-used generic qualitative analysis tool used only as a utility (not a contribution in itself), software should be classified as S3. The paper does not claim to develop any novel software/tool, so S3D1 is more appropriate than S2D1.

This is a literature review article summarizing and synthesizing published experimental data on protein-ionic liquid interactions (solubility data, enzyme activity data, etc.) drawn from a large number of prior studies (e.g., Tables 1-5 compile data from the literature). The authors do not report generating or significantly extending any new research software, nor do they describe using any specific research software package as a methodological tool in their own work (this is a review, not primary research with computational methods). They do, however, use existing research data - compiling and analyzing data (solubility values, activity measurements, structural data) that was generated by other groups' experiments, which were sourced from the literature to inform their review and comparative tables. This constitutes use of existing research data without generating new data themselves. Hence this falls under S3 (No Software) and D2 (Data Used).

This is a qualitative case study based on interviews (25 personal interviews), non-participant observations, archival/document research, and secondary data collected over a longitudinal fieldwork period (2007-2014). This constitutes generated research data (interview transcripts, observational notes, archival material compiled for the study). There is no mention of any research software being created or used (no analysis tools, coding software, or computational methods referenced beyond standard interpretive content analysis). Hence it is No Software, Data Generated.

The paper is an experimental physics study generating new research data (PL spectra, g2(τ) correlation measurements, ODMR spectra, magnetic field dependence data) from novel single-defect measurements in hBN. The data availability statement confirms "datasets generated as part of the current study are available... upon reasonable request," indicating data generation (D1). Regarding software, the authors mention "codes used for the analysis" are available upon request, but this refers to custom analysis scripts (fitting routines, kinetic model simulations) used for processing/analyzing data rather than a standalone research software contribution being presented as a novel tool. There is no claim of developing or significantly extending a software package/tool as a research contribution in its own right - the code appears to be utility analysis scripts (fitting exponential functions, spin Hamiltonian simulations) used to interpret the experimental data, which falls under S3 (software used only as utility, not claimed as a contribution).
